title: I went looking for the poo at Coogee beach but all I found was a beautiful day for a swim

Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian New South Wales I went looking for the poo at Coogee beach but all I found was a beautiful day for a swim Popular ocean beach ranks as Sydney’s worst for faecal pollution – again – but Caitlin Cassidy discovers happy children and families Caitlin Cassidy in Coogee Thu 24 Sep 2026 23.52 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 03.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In the Dharug language spoken by the local Aboriginal people, Coogee, derived from “koojah” or “koojay”, translates to “bad smell”, “rotting seaweed” or “stinking place”. It’s perhaps unsurprising, then, that this week Coogee ranked as the Sydney ocean beach most polluted with faecal matter – again. Coogee’s grading in the 2026 state of the beaches report , an annual survey by the New South Wales environment department, indicated “microbial water quality is susceptible to faecal pollution, particularly after rainfall”. Coogee ranks as Sydney’s worst ocean beach for faecal pollution – again Read more An unsavoury finding indeed, yet one hard to reconcile with the clear blue water seen on a sunny morning at Coogee beach, as hundreds of revellers stretch out on beach towels and paddle gleefully in the ocean. I am here on Friday in search of poo, or any visible signs of the poor water quality grade the popular swimming spot has held for several years now, but instead all I spot are happy children and families. View image in fullscreen Paul Sampson dries off after a swim at Coogee beach: ‘I’ve swum here for about 25 years, and I’m still alive.’ Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian Among them is Paul Sampson, who is towelling himself off after a swim. I ask him if he feels the water is safe, and he replies: “Well, I’ve swum here for about 25 years, and I’m still alive. “Sure, compared to the south coast, the water’s not as clean, but what are you going to do? Generally speaking, the water’s a lot cleaner today to 10, 20 years ago.” He’s not wrong. In 1989, a Turn Back the Tide concert at Bondi beach drew more than 200,000 people protesting severe ocean sewage pollution on Sydney’s coastline. Things have improved since then, but the city is still dealing with the collective trauma of the “mystery balls”. Coogee was one of several beaches that were closed in 2024 and 2025 after poo balls were carried back to shore by waves and wind. The fear of a giant fatberg which, ominously, remains behind a closed door at the Malabar wastewater treatment plant, is alive and real. View image in fullscreen Charlie Herbert says the water quality findings were ‘disappointing’. Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the School of Civil Engineering at the University of Sydney, said the dreaded poo balls were a “negligible contributor” to Coogee’s water quality, as those deep ocean discharges occurred kilometres out to sea. He said Coogee’s “poor” rating was largely due to storm water runoff that brought sewage contamination during times of heavy rain instead of any mass faecal event. Behind this door is the huge fatberg that can’t stop depositing poo balls on Sydney’s beaches Read more After several days without rain, Charlie Herbert doesn’t mind hitting up Coogee’s ocean pool with her young daughter – though she says the water quality findings were “disappointing”. “We only came because we were meeting some friends here – it’s definitely not my first port of call,” she says. “But my kids don’t really like the water, so it’s not too much of a worry.” David Goldstein has lived in the eastern suburbs for four decades and Coogee has always been his beach of choice. On Friday, he’s sitting at a cafe by the water with his dogs, Harriet and Peanut, after completing a swim. View image in fullscreen David Goldstein with his dogs Harriet and Peanut: ‘If a shark won’t get you, pollution will.’ Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian He likes Coogee because of the community – you see the same people all the time, and the pollution issue, he says, isn’t new. “You get some resilience to it,” he says. “I started swimming in the mid-90s and may have got sick once.
